cards.text: Chronicles has been walking through the families of Israel, the man once called Jacob (Genesis 32:28), one son at a time (1 Chronicles 2-4), and now it's Reuben's turn. Reuben is the firstborn, so the birthright should be his. But Chronicles stops RIGHT away to say it went to somebody else.

cards.question: Reuben is Israel's firstborn. So who does his birthright go to?
Reuben loses the birthright because he defiled his father's bed.

cards.text: Joseph's family holds the birthright, but Judah, another son of Israel, prevails over his brothers anyway. No title on the paperwork and STILL on top, while I spent years in a junk drawer losing to a stack of takeout menus.

cards.question: From Judah came a ___, even though the birthright belonged to Joseph.

cards.text: Then come Reuben's sons, Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron and Carmi, and a line of fathers and sons down to Beerah, a Reubenite leader that Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria carried into exile. Beerah's relatives settle in Aroer and as far as Nebo and Baal-meon.

cards.question: The Reubenites also spread east to the edge of the desert that stretches to the Euphrates River, because their ___ had increased in the land of Gilead.

cards.text: In the days of King Saul, the Reubenites, a tribe whose herds already pushed them out to the edge of the desert, go to war against a people called the Hagrites. Remember where we are, friend: so far these folks keep getting BIGGER, not smaller.

cards.question: In the days of King Saul, the Reubenites lose their war with the Hagrites.

cards.text: Next door, in Bashan, live the descendants of Gad, another son of Israel (Genesis 35:26), and Chronicles lists their chiefs and family heads. They spread through Gilead, Bashan and the pasturelands of Sharon, all recorded in the days of Jotham king of Judah and Jeroboam king of Israel.

Now Chronicles zooms out: Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, named for one of Joseph's sons (Genesis 41:51), have 44,760 warriors trained for battle. They go to war against the Hagrites, as well as Jetur, Naphish and Nodab.

cards.question: What do the three tribes do in the middle of the battle against the Hagrites?

answers.text: They call to Judah for help

cards.text: God answers their prayers because they put their trust in Him, and they seize 50,000 camels, 250,000 sheep, 2,000 donkeys and 100,000 captives. I counted dust in a junk drawer for YEARS, friend, and I never once got to 250,000.

cards.question: Many others fell in that battle, because the battle belonged to ___.

cards.text: They hold that land until the exile. Meanwhile the half-tribe of Manasseh is numerous, spread from Bashan all the way up to Mount Hermon, and that is a LOT of cousins to fit in one group chat.

cards.question: The family heads of the half-tribe of Manasseh are remembered as mighty men of valor.
God won a battle for Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh. Right after Manasseh's famous family heads are named, what goes wrong?

answers.text: Turning from God to other gods
Turning on one another in war
Turning the land over to Egypt

cards.question: The gods these families turn to belong to the peoples of the land, peoples God had already destroyed before them.

cards.text: So Pul king of Assyria, also called Tiglath-pileser, the same king who carried off Beerah, takes Reuben, Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh into exile. They end up in Halah, Habor, Hara and by the river of Gozan, and they're still there to this day.

cards.question: Who stirred up the spirit of Pul king of Assyria to carry these tribes into exile?

findings.problem: Joseph is central to the correct answer, but he is introduced only by name. The walkthrough never simply identifies him as a son of Israel, although verse 1 does.

rule.text: The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Calling Judah "another son of Israel" adds a relationship that verse 2 does not state, but no supporting reference is given for that outside fact.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: The clause about the Reubenites' herds pushing them to the edge of the desert retells verse 9, but the card cites only verse 10. Its citation does not cover everything the story card uses.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Calling Saul "King Saul" adds his kingship, which verse 10 does not state, without giving a reference for that outside identification.

rule.text: Facts from outside the passage are fine when they help, like who a new person is or who wrote a letter, with their reference.

findings.problem: Several questions do not carry their own context. Card 12 relies on "the three tribes," card 14 on "that battle," card 18 on "these families," and card 20 on "these tribes," rather than identifying the people or event within the question.

rule.text: Always give context in the question. The story card before it isn't on screen anymore, so the question says who and what. Never "him," "that" or "it" pointing back to a card the baker can't see.

findings.problem: "Meanwhile" adds a simultaneity between the other tribes' occupation and Manasseh's settlement that the text does not state.

rule.text: Times stay true. No time in the text means none added.

findings.problem: Verse 24 is a name list of Manasseh's family heads. Its description is turned into a stand-alone true-or-false question instead of being included as a standout detail in the summary story card for that genealogical stretch.

rule.text: A long stretch never gets a choice card.

findings.problem: The phrase "the same king who carried off Beerah" retells verse 6, but the card cites only verse 26. The citation therefore does not cover all the passage material the card uses.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.
